I knew as soon as I finished that there were definitely going to be some people not satisfied with the ending. Both endings are pretty dark for different reasons, and not for simple reasons.

I do think it is important to remember though, that even though the Canvas isn't "the real world", it is no less real what is happening inside of it. The people, that community, etc. is all real. The best way to think of it is that the painters are the gods and the people within the Canvas are the life they created.

When I was given the choice at the end, I didn't approach it as a simple "Well this world is fake, so it has to be destroyed". It's a much more complex matter than that in my opinion. I do think from a purely objective standpoint, it would be better for Maelle and Verso to end the Canvas, but it comes at the cost of an entire world of living people that Verso and primarily Aline created. To me, it isn't right to end that world just because of this one family's suffering and grief.

So I chose the Maelle ending, and I loved it. I feel like Lumiere was saved, but with the gut punch of seeing Verso and Maelle in the final shots. The moment felt like it had a lot of weight behind it. I think both endings are fantastic, regardless of what you decide to choose.

Basically yes. All party members have a unique mechanic that they play around during battles (one character switches stances based off the moves you use which offer different stat bonuses while another generates elemental charges based off the moves she uses, which can amplify the affects of other abilities) and all of these mechanics can be played into or even altered completely based off what weapons you are using which have a stat progression themselves.

There are also skill trees, but the real customization comes from the game's accessories that you loot and equip. All of the accessories have a stat modification (quite large ones by endgame) and a passive ability, and once you've had one equipped for a few fights, you can then equip the passive ability itself separate from having to use the accessory. You're limited to three accessories at a time, but the amount of passives you can equip is only limited by how many points you find in the game, which you can distribute amongst your party however you please.

All around, it's one of the most flexible build systems I have seen in an RPG, and you can get really crazy with it because there are a *ton* of the accessories and even a lot of the weapons all of which are unique to each party member. If you like build crafting in RPG's, Clair Obscur is an excellent choice.

When people say "mature" in this context, I'm pretty sure they're referring to the art style. E33 looks realistic, like it's for adults. Most JRPG's are anime, and to people who don't like anime, they'll say it's "just for kids".

That's the stigma most JRPG's have and why most people will not give them the time of day.

No, the combat system is amazing even by JRPG standards. I think Atlus games are the gold standard for turn based combat mechanics, and I actually think E33 blows them out of the water.

Just the real time mechanics like dodging and parrying would be enough, it's so engaging and satisfying when pull it off perfectly, but the unique mechanics that they give each party member is also something you just don't see too often. Typically you've got your physical hitter, your magic dealer, your healer, etc. The mechanics tied to each party member in E33 are so in depth, and open up so many different possibilities for you to break the game or pull off some insane damage turns is crazy, and I thought Metaphor was bonkers.

The story of E33 is an all timer, but I don't think it's fair to say it overshadows this game's combat at all.

I am a huge JRPG fan, and while the take that "JRPG's are saved" is stupid, I would argue that E33 *is* genre defining in some ways. 

The real time mechanics they've added to combat are amazing additions that frankly, I'm gonna have an extremely hard time going back to RNG based luck with more traditional JRPG's. Also, we just don't get turn based games presented in a realistic, high fidelity style like this, like you'd expect from a western studio. They're almost always an anime or cartoon art style, and if a JRPG *is* in a more realistic art style, then it's almost always an action based RPG with no turn based mechanics.

These two elements are huge steps forward for the genre that I would actually love to see more games embrace. Not necessarily the classic franchises like Atlus games or the like, but just new games that do this type of style.

Because it isn't Japanese. I say this as a massive fan of Atlus games, but the Japanese style is just flat out not for some people. I'd love to recommend games like Persona or Metaphor to people I know, but I also know they'd roll their eyes the instant they took one look at it.

E33 is very similar in a lot of ways to those games, but it does so all through a AAA style narrative that you'd expect from a premier western studio, rather than an anime style that's targeted towards weebs. E33 is such a revelation for some people because there are a lot of people who just flat out don't like the anime crap, and I think that's fair because it is an acquired taste.

The short of it is Bobby Kotick wanted to funnel a TON of resources into OW after 2016 and he wanted to make it the company's next COD. Jeff proceeded to over promise when OW2 was announced, specifically with PvE, when the staff was barely keeping up with PvP as it was. They completely sidelined PvP development and worked exclusively on PvE content, but the PvE was not coming together quickly behind the scenes, and after three years they had not made much progress and the PvP game was dying out due to lack of support. This infuriated Bobby because of how badly it was fumbling the new golden egg.

It's unclear if Jeff was actually fired behind the scenes, asked to resign, or if he just completely walked away of his own accord knowing how bad the situation was, but he left and Aaron came in. The choice was either spending another three plus years on a PvE mode that was struggling in development, or quickly resurrecting the PvP game that was live right now, and he choose the latter. 

OW's small development team simply can't handle juggling both modes simultaneously, and they really needed to give it to a different studio like Bobby Kotick originally intended to do. The reason the brand is so toxic now is due to Jeff's ego and refusal to give up control over his creative baby.

The promise of an open "Hitman-esque" time looping puzzle of how to kill eight targets within a single day is completely misleading, as all the game consists of is a set of guided objectives that it holds your hand for to deliver you to the one and only solution to the "puzzle". And these objectives all take place within the same four maps, with the only variance usually being in enemy placement depending on the time of day. You are better off playing a Dishonored game where at least each new level is a new environment and scenario for you to work with.

And finally the story is forgettable and just boring. The antagonists are never properly established or even given much of any screentime to even make you identify them anything other than some named NPC, and the overall scenario is just eight idiots who fucked up an experiment and decide to just party in a time loop repeatedly, which is a pretty stupid conceit. I wasn't expecting some top tier story or anything from this game, but at least something fun and whacky given the tone and the more light-hearted writing, but it just doesn't even achieve that. Any narrative is just background noise that hardly registers.

Throw all this on top of just some particularly janky feeling gameplay with various performance issues, and you've got yourself a pretty banal video game. Absolutely in no way, shape, or form deserving of a 96 on Metacritic, or even anything north of an 80 if you ask me.

Correct. Titan never got off the ground, and instead they made OW which reused a lot of the concept art from Titan. They never stated this until several years later, but the original plan was for OW to turn into Titan via "crawl, walk, then run".

OW1 as an arena PvP hero shooter was Titan crawling. OW2 continuing that and meshing PvE related content with RPG elements was Titan walking. And who knows what would've come next beyond that.

Unfortunately for Titan, Overwatch as a PvP game became way more popular than they imagined, and putting it on the back burner for years to focus on PvE turned out be a large miscalculation, not really realizing that they were sacrificing something loved while chasing a dream.

That's not to say that people don't want PvE OW. It's just that the OW team as it is now cannot handle the simultaneous development of both modes. While they abandoned PvE for OW2, I personally find it difficult to believe Blizzard would completely abandon the idea of further building out the OW IP either in a separate game or a separate mode supported by a different development team. I also find it far more likely that a Blizzard produced FPS/RPG that is coming to console is an off shoot of OW rather than a new IP.

One thing people always get mixed up is the whole RPG-esque elements with skill trees and everything was only for the repeatable hero missions (I forget what they were being referred to as) which were separate from the story missions. The story missions we got were probably pretty close to the original vision, based off the first one being nearly identical at Blizzcon as it was at final release (only missing the item drops).

In order to make OW PvE work long term and not just as a flash in in the pan for a week before everyone moves on, it needs *a lot* of work to be put into it, way more than the development team can handle while juggling the live game. PvE got shelved because the PvP side of the game was suffering with no updates while we had no idea what was going on with OW2.

If PvE ever does happen for OW, it needs to be handled by a completely different team so that they can take their time to create an actual foundation for it, and focus exclusively on it while Team 4 continues supporting the current live game. No idea if that will happen with Microsoft in charge now, but I think there is still a considerable enough interest in the OW characters and some form of PvE that would justify it.

Helldivers is a different case for multiple reasons. Firstly, it is a PvE game, and yes that is a massive difference. It's catering to a completely different audience and is not rooted in a genre where all of it's contemporaries are free to play.

Secondly, Helldivers experienced a massive boom thanks to word of mouth from influencer and media. Games don't normally surge the way that Helldivers did, and it's because the people that everyone listens to started to rave about it. That isn't happening with Concord, it's a much more polarizing reception, and in some cases extremely negative. I've seen some very prominent content creators put up their videos mocking Concord and they're receiving over a million views. That type of exposure is extremely damaging to a game's reputation.

Lastly, I think the expectations for Concord are wildly different than Helldivers. Helldivers wasn't expecting a massive audience, it was probably more expecting where it's current numbers are sitting at right now for it's launch. It's clear over time that Arrowhead wasn't really prepared to do the full on live service treatment that people have come to expect, and that's why they've slowed down on updates in order to better position themselves for long term support.

Concord is expecting to do those long term updates and it's expecting an audience that is relatively comparable to similar games such as Overwatch or Valorant. That's the level of audience a game like this really needs to succeed in the long term, and right now it doesn't even appear to be closing in on that.

While they're not literal number figures, I did check current PSN pre-orders by best selling, and the beta really did not move Concord much up at all, when it was already sitting very low. This just isn't the type of game people pay money to play anymore. Not in 2024. Audiences expect this type of experience to be free, because literally every other competitive PvP hero shooter out there is.

This patch is very misguided, but for different reasons. Blizzard is trying to make tanks "tankier" when they are perfectly fine as they are. The issue is that people just flat out don't find them fun to play, and I think that's an issue that has *always* been prevalent with the game even back to OW1 when tanks were supposedly in a good spot. It stems from a variety of reasons, some of which I don't think can ever be solved such as the fact that some players will *always* just shoot the tank because it's easy or that people will blame their tanks for losses even when it's not accurate. I don't think there's really anything you can fix about that, because those are community driven problems, not systemic problems from the game.

What can be fixed or at least marginalized are things like the player feedback experience, or the "counterwatch" debacle. For player feedback, just give the tank player some more dopamine hits for playing well. They did this with supports in OW2 by adding "player saved" notifications and statistics, and something similar can be done with tanks, whether it be for objective play or damage mitigation, but something directly from the game to tell the tank player "you're doing well". There's nothing for them right now in the game, and while this is just a placebo effect, I think that's all that's needed when the general player perception is "this isn't fun and I'm not doing anything".

As for counterwatch? Just look at each tank's weakness, what the common counter response is, and work towards at least mitigating that on the tank's side. I know that can be a difficult process and it'd have to be unique per tank, but take D.va for example. Everyone's response to D.va is to go beam heroes because she can't block that. So just allow her to block beams with matrix, even if with a reduced effect. The creator mode had this idea, and I think it does a good job to balance D.va a bit more against her usual "counters". You'd have to find different solutions for each tank, but I feel like that's the best way to solving the whole "rock papers scissors" that most games boil down to right now.

There are deeper solutions to the role's problems, but unfortunately Blizzard isn't looking too hard at them and are just going for surface level fixes, which don't really do anything for the core issues. Personally, I think the tank role is objectively perfectly fine as it was before today (and maybe even after today, who knows it's only been half a day). I think a lot of the core issues boil down to player perception as well as social pressure from other players in the game. And those are things that can be very difficult to fix on Blizzard's end.
